name: Modern World History
author: Recurse
subject: humanities
description: Industrialization, revolutions, nationalism and empire, the world wars, the Cold War and the world since 1991.

lesson.intro: The modern world was shaped by a chain of upheavals: new machines, new ideas about who should rule, two world wars and a long superpower rivalry. Follow that chain from about 1760 to today, with a focus on why things happened.
objectives: Explain why the Industrial Revolution began in Britain and how it changed work
Compare the causes and results of the American and French Revolutions
Trace how nationalism, empire and alliances led to World War I, and its peace to World War II
Describe the Cold War, decolonization and European integration after 1945
Place major events since 1991 in context, from globalization to the war in Ukraine

sections.title: The Industrial Revolution
sections.key: Starting in Britain around 1760, machines and steam power moved work from homes into factories, grew cities fast and began sustained economic growth.
sections.body:
Before about 1760, most cloth was spun and woven by hand in homes and small workshops: the **domestic system**. Machines such as the spinning jenny, the water frame and the power loom moved production into **factories**.

James Watt's improved steam engine (patented 1769) let factories run on coal instead of water, and steam railways from the 1820s cut the cost of moving goods and people.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

Factory towns were crowded and unhealthy. Children worked long hours in mills and mines until laws such as Britain's **Factory Act of 1833** began to limit child labor. Workers formed **trade unions**, and critics such as Karl Marx attacked industrial capitalism.

Over the long run, output per person grew faster than ever before, and industry spread to Europe, the United States and Japan.

visual.title: Why Britain first?
rows: Plentiful coal and iron, often close together
Cheap fuel and materials
Capital and markets from overseas trade and empire
Money to invest and buyers to sell to
Better farming
Fed a growing population and freed workers for industry
High wages and cheap coal
Made labor-saving machines profitable
Patents and secure property rights
Rewarded invention
visual.caption: Historians stress that these causes worked together.

items.title: Domestic system
points: Work at home or in small workshops

items.title: Factory system
points: Work in mills with machines driven by water, then steam
Wages for long, fixed hours set by the factory clock
Workers crowd into fast-growing towns such as Manchester

sections.pitfall: Thinking of the Industrial Revolution as one invention or one moment. It was a long process with several causes, and it spread over more than a century.

check.question: By the mid-1800s, what powered most British factories and railways?
choices: Electric motors and dynamos
Steam engines burning coal
Oil-fired combustion engines
Windmills and wind pumps
check.explanation: Watt's improved steam engine freed factories from rivers and water wheels, and steam locomotives drove the railways. Electricity and oil became important only later in the century and after.

sections.title: The American and French Revolutions
sections.key: Both revolutions applied Enlightenment ideas of natural rights and government by consent, and America's war, which France helped pay for, pushed France toward bankruptcy.
sections.body:
Both revolutions drew on **Enlightenment** ideas: people have natural rights, and a government's authority comes from the **consent of the governed**. Both also began with a government short of money.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

Consequences: hereditary privilege was challenged across Europe, the **Napoleonic Code** spread equality before the law, and ideas of citizenship and nationalism shaped the century that followed.

visual.title: The American Revolution
rows: The Seven Years' War leaves Britain deep in debt
The Stamp Act and Townshend duties tax the colonies, which elect no members of Parliament: "no taxation without representation"
Fighting begins
July 4, 1776
The Continental Congress adopts the Declaration of Independence
With French help, the Americans win at Yorktown
The Treaty of Paris recognizes the United States
A constitution creates a republic with separated powers

visual.title: The French Revolution
rows: Royal debt, made worse by aiding the Americans. The clergy and nobility pay little tax, so the Third Estate, everyone else, carries the burden
Poor harvests push up bread prices
May 1789
Louis XVI calls the Estates-General; the Third Estate declares itself a National Assembly
Parisians storm the Bastille
August 1789
Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen
The monarchy is abolished, the king executed (1793), and the Reign of Terror kills tens of thousands
Napoleon Bonaparte seizes power

sections.pitfall: Mixing up the order. The American Revolution (1775 to 1783) came first, and its cost helped push France toward bankruptcy and its own revolution in 1789.

check.question: How did France's support for the American Revolution help bring on the French Revolution?
choices: American troops invaded France to spread revolution
It persuaded Louis XVI to give up his throne
The United States demanded that France become a republic
It added heavily to the French crown's debt
check.explanation: Fighting Britain in America was expensive, and the extra debt deepened France's financial crisis in the 1780s. French soldiers returning from America also brought home ideas about liberty.

sections.title: Nationalism and empire in the 1800s
sections.key: Nationalism united Germany and Italy but strained multiethnic empires, while industrial powers used new technology to carve up Africa and force open China.
sections.body:
In 1800 there was no Germany or Italy, only dozens of separate states. By 1914 both were powerful nations, and Europeans ruled almost all of Africa.

**Nationalism**, the idea that a people sharing a language and culture should have its own state, spread after the French Revolution. It united some lands and split others: in Austria-Hungary and the Ottoman Empire, Serbs, Greeks, Czechs and others demanded independence, making the Balkans unstable.

**Imperialism** peaked. Industrial powers wanted raw materials, markets and prestige, and steamships, railways, the telegraph, quinine against malaria and the machine gun made conquest easier. By 1914 only **Ethiopia and Liberia** in Africa were still independent.

[[visual]]

Japan took its own path: after the **Meiji Restoration** of 1868 it industrialized, rebuilt its forces on Western lines and became an imperial power itself.

This set the stage for 1914: a powerful new Germany, colonial rivalry and Balkan tension.

visual.title: Nations and empires, 1839 to 1905
rows: First Opium War: Britain forces China to open ports on unequal terms (a second war follows in 1856-60)
Britain begins direct rule of India
Italy is unified by Piedmont's prime minister Cavour and Garibaldi's campaigns in the south: kingdom proclaimed 1861, Rome the capital in 1871
The Meiji Restoration begins Japan's modernization
January 1871
The German Empire is proclaimed at Versailles, after Prussian chancellor Otto von Bismarck's three short wars, the last against France
The Berlin Conference sets rules for claiming African territory
Japan defeats China, then Russia

sections.pitfall: Treating nationalism only as a uniting force. The same idea that built Germany and Italy helped break apart multiethnic empires such as Austria-Hungary and the Ottoman Empire.

check.question: Which leader is most closely associated with the unification of Germany?
choices: Giuseppe Garibaldi
Napoleon Bonaparte
Otto von Bismarck
Klemens von Metternich
check.explanation: Bismarck, Prussia's chancellor, unified Germany through three short wars, ending with the proclamation of the German Empire in 1871. Garibaldi fought for Italian unification, and Metternich, an Austrian statesman, worked to hold back nationalism.

sections.title: World War I: causes and outcomes
sections.key: Alliances, militarism, imperialism and nationalism made a wide war likely; the assassination at Sarajevo in June 1914 was only the trigger.
sections.body:
Historians group the long-term causes of World War I under four headings, the fuel:

[[visual]]

The spark came on June 28, 1914, when **Gavrilo Princip**, a Bosnian Serb nationalist, shot Archduke **Franz Ferdinand**, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, in Sarajevo. Alliances turned it into a European war within about a week:

[[visual 2]]

Germany's **Schlieffen Plan**, to beat France fast by going through Belgium and then face Russia, failed. The Western Front settled into **trench warfare**. The United States joined the Allies in 1917, Russia left in early 1918, and the **armistice** of November 11, 1918 ended the fighting.

[[visual 3]]

visual.title: Four long-term causes
rows: Militarism
An arms race, including the Anglo-German naval race, and rigid war plans
Alliances
The Triple Entente (France, Russia, Britain) against the Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy). Italy stayed neutral in 1914 and joined the Allies in 1915
Imperialism
Rivalry over colonies and influence
Nationalism
National pride and grievances, especially among the Slavic peoples of the Balkans

steps.label: July 28: Austria-Hungary declares war on Serbia
Germany declares war on Russia and France

visual.title: What the war left behind
rows: Deaths
More than 8 million soldiers and millions of civilians
Empires
Four collapsed: German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman. New states such as Poland and Czechoslovakia appeared
Treaty of Versailles (1919)
Germany accepts responsibility for the war ("war guilt"), pays reparations, loses land and all its colonies, and may keep an army of only 100,000
League of Nations
Created to keep the peace, but the United States never joined
Russia
The tsar falls in February 1917. In October, Lenin's Bolsheviks seize power and make a separate peace with Germany (March 1918). The Soviet Union forms in 1922

sections.pitfall: Treating the assassination as the cause of the war. It was the trigger; alliances, militarism, imperialism and nationalism explain why it became a world war.

check.question: What was the Schlieffen Plan?
choices: A British plan to blockade Germany's North Sea ports
Russia's plan to strike Austria-Hungary before Germany could help
Germany's plan to beat France fast via Belgium, then face Russia
An American peace plan based on national self-determination
check.explanation: Expecting a two-front war, Germany planned to knock France out quickly by marching through Belgium. The plan stalled at the Marne in September 1914, leading to trench stalemate, and the invasion of Belgium brought Britain into the war.

sections.title: Between the wars and World War II
sections.key: Resentment of Versailles, the Great Depression, a weak League of Nations and appeasement together turned grievance into a second world war.
sections.body:
The peace did not last. Many Germans resented the Treaty of Versailles, hyperinflation in 1923 wiped out savings, and after the Wall Street Crash of October 1929 the **Great Depression** brought mass unemployment. Desperate voters turned to extremists: Mussolini had ruled Italy since 1922, and Hitler became Germany's chancellor in January 1933.

The **League of Nations** had no army, needed its members to agree on sanctions, and lacked the United States. It did little when Japan invaded Manchuria (1931) or Italy invaded Ethiopia (1935). Britain and France followed **appeasement**: giving in to some of Hitler's demands to avoid war.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

An estimated 70 to 85 million people died, most of them civilians. In the **Holocaust**, Nazi Germany and its collaborators systematically murdered about six million Jews, along with millions of others.

visual.title: The road to war
rows: The Nazis become the largest party in parliament
Munich Agreement: Britain and France accept Germany taking the Sudetenland in Czechoslovakia
March 1939
Germany seizes the rest of Czechoslovakia, and appeasement ends
August 1939
Germany signs a non-aggression pact with the Soviet Union
September 1, 1939
Germany invades Poland; Britain and France declare war two days later

visual.title: Turning points
rows: June 1941
Germany invades the Soviet Union
December 7, 1941
Japan attacks the US base at Pearl Harbor, bringing the United States into the war
Soviet victory at Stalingrad
June 1944
D-Day landings in Normandy
May 1945
Germany surrenders
August 1945
Japan surrenders, after the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and the Soviet declaration of war

sections.pitfall: Blaming World War II on the Treaty of Versailles alone. Resentment mattered, but the Great Depression, the League's weakness and appeasement turned grievance into war.

check.question: What brought the United States into World War II as a combatant?
choices: Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941
Germany's invasion of Poland in September 1939
The sinking of the liner Lusitania by a U-boat
The fall of France to Germany in June 1940
check.explanation: The US stayed out of the fighting until Japan's surprise attack on Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941; Germany declared war on the US four days later. The Lusitania was sunk in 1915, during World War I.

sections.title: After 1945: the UN, decolonization, Cold War, EU
sections.key: After 1945 the UN, decolonization, the Cold War and European integration reshaped the world, until the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991.
sections.body:
The **United Nations** was founded in 1945 to prevent another world war. Learning from the League, it gave five main victors (the US, the Soviet Union, Britain, France and China) permanent Security Council seats with a **veto**, keeping the great powers inside the system.

**Decolonization**: from 1945 to the 1970s most colonies in Asia and Africa became independent. The war had weakened Britain, France and the Netherlands, independence movements had grown, and both superpowers opposed old-style empires.

[[visual]]

In the **Cold War** the US and its allies faced the Soviet Union and its allies: capitalist democracy against one-party communism. The US followed **containment**. Nuclear weapons made direct war suicidal, so they competed through arms and space races, propaganda and **proxy wars** such as Korea and Vietnam.

[[visual 2]]

[[visual 3]]

visual.title: Decolonization
rows: India and Pakistan become independent, in a partition that uprooted millions
Algeria's long, violent war of independence against France
17 African countries gain independence in a single year
visual.caption: Borders drawn by colonial powers often left lasting conflicts.

visual.title: The Cold War, about 1947 to 1991
rows: NATO is founded
The Warsaw Pact is formed
The Berlin Wall is built
The Cuban Missile Crisis: the closest to nuclear war
Mikhail Gorbachev becomes Soviet leader, begins reforms, and later refuses to use force to hold Eastern Europe
Communist governments in Eastern Europe fall, and the Berlin Wall is opened on November 9
Germany reunifies
December 1991
The Soviet Union dissolves

steps.label: 1951: European Coal and Steel Community
steps.detail: Six countries pool coal and steel to make war between France and Germany practically impossible

sections.pitfall: Picturing the Cold War as having no fighting. The superpowers never fought each other directly, but proxy wars in Korea, Vietnam and Afghanistan killed millions.

check.question: In which year did the Soviet Union dissolve?
check.explanation: The Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991. In 1989 the Berlin Wall opened, in 1985 Gorbachev came to power, and in 1961 the Wall was built.

sections.title: Since 1991: globalization and new fault lines
sections.key: Since 1991, globalization has tied economies together while new shocks, from 9/11 and the 2008 crash to COVID-19 and Russia's invasion of Ukraine, reshaped the world.
sections.body:
The end of the Cold War looked to many like the start of a calmer, more connected world. Trade, travel and the internet did tie economies together, but new conflicts and shocks followed.

**Globalization** sped up. China joined the World Trade Organization in 2001 and became the world's largest manufacturer and its second largest economy at market exchange rates. Hundreds of millions of people across Asia escaped extreme poverty. The **World Wide Web** (Tim Berners-Lee, 1989, public in the early 1990s) and later the smartphone changed how people work, shop and get news.

[[visual]]

Historians handle recent events carefully, because their consequences are still unfolding. The same tools apply: look for long-term causes, immediate triggers and unintended consequences.

visual.title: Since 1991
rows: Yugoslavia breaks up, bringing war and genocide to Bosnia
Genocide in Rwanda: about 800,000 people killed
The World Trade Organization is founded
The euro is launched (notes and coins in 2002)
September 11: al-Qaeda attacks kill nearly 3,000 people in the US, leading to war in Afghanistan. China joins the WTO
War in Iraq
The EU admits ten new members, most of them former communist states
Losses on US mortgage-linked securities set off a financial crisis: the deepest global recession since the 1930s
Russia annexes Crimea
The United Kingdom votes to leave the EU
The UK leaves in January, leaving the EU with 27 members. The COVID-19 pandemic kills millions and shuts down much of the world economy
February 2022
Russia launches a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Europe's largest war since 1945

sections.pitfall: Assuming the end of the Cold War ended major wars. Conflicts in the Balkans, Rwanda, Afghanistan, Iraq and Ukraine all came after 1991.

check.question: In what year did the United Kingdom formally leave the European Union?
check.explanation: The UK left on January 31, 2020, after years of negotiation. 2016 was the year of the referendum in which voters chose to leave, which is the usual mix-up.

keyTerms.definition: Production in large buildings where workers ran machines driven by water or steam, replacing work done at home.
An 18th-century movement that stressed reason, natural rights and government by consent.
Strong loyalty to one's nation and the belief that each nation should govern itself.
Payments a defeated country must make for war damage, as Germany was required to after 1919.
Giving in to an aggressor's demands to avoid war, as Britain and France did with Hitler in the 1930s.
The process by which colonies became independent states, mostly between 1945 and the 1970s.
The US Cold War policy of stopping communism from spreading to new countries.
A conflict in which rival powers back opposing sides instead of fighting each other directly.
Extending a country's power by taking control of other lands, as European powers did in Africa and Asia in the 1800s.
An agreement to stop fighting, such as the one that ended World War I on November 11, 1918.
The growing connection of economies and societies through trade, investment, travel and communication, which sped up after 1991.

summary: From about 1760, Britain led the move to factories, cities and sustained growth.
The American (1776) and French (1789) Revolutions spread rights and popular rule.
Nationalism united Germany and Italy and strained empires; Europe carved up Africa.
Alliances turned Sarajevo into World War I; Versailles, the Depression and appeasement led to World War II.
After 1945: the UN, decolonization, the Cold War and the EU. The Soviet Union fell in 1991.
Since 1991: globalization, 9/11, the 2008 crash, COVID-19 and the war in Ukraine.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend how the way World War I ended helped lead to World War II, using at least two concrete links between them.

questions.question: Why did the Industrial Revolution begin in Britain rather than elsewhere?
choices: Its government designed, built and ran the first factories itself
It had the largest population and cheapest labor in Europe
Coal, trade capital, big markets and high wages made machines pay off
It imported cheap steam engines that had been invented in France
questions.explanation: Historians stress a combination: accessible coal and iron, capital and markets from trade, a growing population fed by better farming, and wages that were high compared with the price of coal, which made labor-saving machines profitable. British labor was relatively expensive, not cheap, and private entrepreneurs, not the state, built the factories.

questions.question: Explain how the move from the domestic system to the factory system changed workers' lives.
questions.answer: Work moved from homes and small workshops into factories with machines driven by water or steam. Workers earned wages for long, fixed hours set by the factory clock and crowded into fast-growing towns, conditions that led in time to trade unions and laws such as Britain's 1833 Factory Act.
questions.explanation: The factory system concentrated machines, workers and power in one place. Output rose, but where and how people lived and worked changed, and those conditions drove the first labor laws and unions.

questions.question: In what year did the Continental Congress adopt the Declaration of Independence?
questions.explanation: The Declaration was adopted on July 4, 1776, a year after fighting began in 1775. Britain recognized American independence only in the Treaty of Paris in 1783.

questions.question: What was the main grievance behind the American colonists' slogan "No taxation without representation"?
choices: The colonies paid far higher taxes than people living in Britain
Parliament taxed the colonies, but they elected no members to it
Colonists were being drafted to fight Britain's wars in Europe
France was imposing taxes on American trade with Britain
questions.explanation: Colonists objected that Parliament, where they had no members, was imposing taxes such as the Stamp Act. They actually paid less tax than people in Britain; the dispute was about consent, not the size of the bill.

questions.question: In what year did Parisians storm the Bastille, an event often used to mark the start of the French Revolution?
questions.explanation: The Bastille fell on July 14, 1789, about two months after Louis XVI had called the Estates-General. France still celebrates July 14 as its national day.

questions.question: Which combination of pressures led Louis XVI to call the Estates-General in 1789?
choices: A Protestant revolt demanding freedom of worship
Defeat in the Napoleonic Wars and foreign occupation
A demand by peasants to restore the old feudal dues
Heavy royal debt, an unfair tax system and costly bread
questions.explanation: The crown was close to bankruptcy, partly from wars including its support for the Americans; the clergy and nobility paid little tax; and poor harvests had pushed bread prices up. The Napoleonic Wars came later, after Napoleon took power in 1799.

questions.question: What was the immediate trigger of World War I?
choices: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in June 1914
Germany's invasion of Poland in September 1939
The sinking of the passenger liner Lusitania in 1915
The Russian Revolution and the fall of the Tsar in 1917
questions.explanation: On 28 June 1914 a Bosnian Serb nationalist killed the heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, and Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia a month later. The invasion of Poland started World War II, and the Lusitania sinking and the Russian Revolution came after World War I had begun.

questions.question: Why did a conflict between Austria-Hungary and Serbia turn into a war across Europe within about a week?
choices: Serbia launched surprise invasions of both Germany and France
Alliance ties pulled in Russia, Germany, France and Britain in turn
The League of Nations ordered all of its members to take sides
All of Europe's monarchs agreed to declare war on the same day
questions.explanation: Russia backed Serbia, Germany backed Austria-Hungary and declared war on Russia and France, and Germany's invasion of Belgium brought Britain in. The League of Nations did not exist until 1920.

questions.question: Which was a term of the Treaty of Versailles (1919)?
choices: Germany received Alsace-Lorraine from France
Germany was allowed to keep its overseas colonies
Germany accepted blame for the war and agreed to pay reparations
Germany became a founding member of the League of Nations
questions.explanation: Article 231, the "war guilt" clause, made Germany accept responsibility for the war's damage, which justified reparations. Germany lost Alsace-Lorraine to France and all its colonies, and it was not admitted to the League until 1926.

questions.question: Which development did most to help extremist parties such as the Nazis win mass support in Germany in the early 1930s?
choices: Mass unemployment and poverty during the Great Depression
A rapid rise in wages and exports after 1929
The Allies' decision to cancel all reparations in 1919
Germany's success in gaining new colonies in Africa
questions.explanation: After the Wall Street Crash of 1929, American loans dried up and German unemployment rose to about six million by 1932. Desperate voters turned to parties promising radical change, and the Nazis became the largest party in parliament in 1932. Reparations were imposed in 1919, not canceled.

questions.question: What name is given to the policy Britain and France followed in the 1930s of giving in to some of Hitler's demands to avoid war?
questions.explanation: Appeasement peaked with the Munich Agreement of 1938, which let Germany take the Sudetenland. It ended when Germany seized the rest of Czechoslovakia in March 1939.

questions.question: Why did the League of Nations fail to stop aggression in the 1930s?
choices: Its own army was too small to fight Japan and Italy at once
It was dissolved soon after the Wall Street Crash of 1929
Germany and Italy used vetoes on its Security Council
It had no army, depended on agreement, and lacked the United States
questions.explanation: The League could only call for sanctions, which members often ignored, and the United States never joined. It did little when Japan invaded Manchuria in 1931 or Italy invaded Ethiopia in 1935. A Security Council with vetoes belongs to the later United Nations.
questions.concept: failure of the League of Nations

questions.question: How did the founders of the United Nations try to avoid the League of Nations' main weakness?
choices: They gave the UN a large permanent army of its own
They kept the defeated powers and the Soviet Union out
They required every member to agree before any action
They gave the great powers permanent Security Council vetoes
questions.explanation: The League failed partly because great powers stayed out or left. The UN gave five main victors permanent seats and a veto so they would stay inside the system. The UN has no standing army of its own, and the Soviet Union was a founding member.

questions.question: Which factor helped speed up decolonization after 1945?
choices: World War II had weakened the European colonial powers
Colonies had become more profitable than ever before
The UN Charter required colonies to stay under European rule
Both superpowers strongly supported Europe's empires
questions.explanation: Britain, France and the Netherlands came out of the war exhausted and in debt, while independence movements had grown stronger. The UN Charter supported self-determination, and both the US and the Soviet Union opposed old-style empires.

questions.question: Explain why the Cold War is called "cold".
questions.answer: The United States and the Soviet Union never fought each other directly. Nuclear weapons made a direct war potentially suicidal for both, so they competed through an arms race, the space race, rival alliances, propaganda and proxy wars such as Korea and Vietnam.
questions.explanation: "Cold" means no direct fighting between the superpowers. The rivalry was still deadly in proxy wars, and in the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962 it came close to nuclear war.

questions.question: In what year was the Berlin Wall opened, as communist governments in Eastern Europe fell?
questions.explanation: The Wall opened on November 9, 1989. Germany reunified in 1990, and the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991, ending the Cold War.

questions.question: What was the original aim of the European Coal and Steel Community, founded in 1951?
choices: To replace national currencies with a single European money
To bind France and Germany together so war between them became impossible
To form a military alliance of Western Europe against the Soviet Union
To give Britain control of Europe's coal and steel supplies
questions.explanation: Coal and steel were the raw materials of war, so putting them under shared control tied France, West Germany and four neighbors together. The euro came decades later, the Western military alliance was NATO, and Britain did not join until 1973.

questions.question: Put these events in chronological order, earliest first.
items: The proclamation of the German Empire
The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand
questions.explanation: 1776, 1789, 1871, 1914, 1929 and 1939. Each link matters: the American war helped bankrupt France, a unified Germany changed Europe's balance of power, and the Depression after 1929 helped bring extremists to power.

questions.question: Put these Cold War events in order, earliest first.
questions.explanation: 1949, 1955, 1961, 1962, 1985, 1989 and 1991. The Warsaw Pact answered NATO, the Wall went up a year before the missile crisis, and Gorbachev's reforms led within six years to the Wall opening and the Soviet collapse.

questions.question: Match each leader to the country they led.
questions.explanation: Bismarck unified Germany, Louis XVI was king when the French Revolution broke out, Gorbachev was the last Soviet leader, Mussolini ruled Fascist Italy from 1922, and Japan modernized under Emperor Meiji after 1868.

questions.question: Match each treaty or agreement to what it did.

pairs.right: Made Germany accept war guilt and pay reparations

questions.explanation: Treaties make good anchors for a timeline: 1783 ended the American Revolution, 1919 ended World War I on harsh terms, 1938 was the high point of appeasement, and 1957 and 1992 were steps in European integration.

questions.question: In what year was the German Empire proclaimed at Versailles?
questions.explanation: After Prussia defeated France, the German Empire was proclaimed in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles in January 1871. Germany later signed the 1919 peace treaty in the same room, a deliberate reversal.

questions.question: By 1914, which two African countries were still independent of European rule?
choices: Egypt and Morocco
Ethiopia and Liberia
Nigeria and Kenya
South Africa and Algeria
questions.explanation: Ethiopia defeated an Italian invasion at Adwa in 1896, and Liberia, founded by freed American slaves, kept its independence. Egypt and Morocco were under British and French control, and the others were colonies.

questions.question: Select every factor that historians commonly link to the outbreak of World War II.
choices: German resentment of the Treaty of Versailles
The Great Depression
The weakness of the League of Nations
The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand
The Cuban Missile Crisis
Britain and France's policy of appeasement
questions.explanation: Versailles left resentment, the Depression brought extremists to power, the League could not stop aggression, and appeasement let Hitler expand. The assassination triggered World War I, and the missile crisis came in 1962, during the Cold War.

questions.question: How did Japan's path in the late 1800s differ from that of most of Asia?
choices: It was colonized by Britain after the Opium Wars
It became a communist state under Soviet influence
It modernized rapidly after 1868 and became an imperial power itself
It cut off all foreign trade until the end of World War II
questions.explanation: After the Meiji Restoration, Japan built industry and a modern army and navy, then defeated China (1895) and Russia (1905) and took colonies of its own. China, not Japan, lost the Opium Wars, and the Soviet Union did not exist until 1922.

questions.question: How many member states has the European Union had since the United Kingdom left in 2020?
questions.explanation: The EU had 28 members before Brexit and 27 after the UK left on January 31, 2020. The six founding countries of the 1950s have grown through several rounds of enlargement, the biggest in 2004.

questions.question: A historian says, "The shots at Sarajevo were the spark, not the fuel." What does she mean?
choices: The assassination had nothing to do with the outbreak of war
The assassination triggered the war, but deeper causes such as alliances and militarism made a wide war likely
The war was caused mainly by shortages of coal and oil
Serbia alone was responsible for the war that followed
questions.explanation: Historians separate triggers from long-term causes. The assassination set events moving, but the alliance system, arms race, imperial rivalry and nationalism are why a Balkan crisis became a world war within weeks.

questions.question: Which of these happened first?
choices: China joins the World Trade Organization
The September 11 attacks
The euro is launched as a currency
The global financial crisis
questions.explanation: The euro launched in 1999. The September 11 attacks came in September 2001, China joined the WTO in December 2001, and the financial crisis struck in 2008.

questions.question: Why did Russia leave World War I in early 1918?
choices: Germany had already surrendered on the Eastern Front
The Bolsheviks, who seized power in 1917, made a separate peace with Germany
The United States ordered Russia to withdraw its troops
Russia had already achieved all of its war aims
questions.explanation: War losses and shortages brought revolution in 1917. Lenin's Bolsheviks had promised peace, and in March 1918 they signed the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk with Germany, giving up large territories. Germany did not surrender until November 1918.
